reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with severe, deep, boring ocular pain that is often worse at night, may radiate to the face or jaw, and characteristically disturbs sleep
The redness has a bluish or violaceous hue from involvement of the deep scleral vessels, unlike the bright red of episcleritis
Scleral vessels do not blanch with topical phenylephrine, which helps distinguish scleritis from episcleritis
Classified into anterior (diffuse, nodular, or necrotising) and posterior forms; necrotising scleritis is the most destructive and sight-threatening
Scleromalacia perforans is a painless necrotising form seen in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis
Roughly half of cases are associated with systemic disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis and ANCA-associated vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Posterior scleritis can mimic other conditions with proptosis, pain on eye movement, and disc swelling, and is confirmed on ultrasound (T-sign)
Management is with systemic anti-inflammatory therapy: oral NSAIDs for milder disease and systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppression for necrotising or refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Scleritis is inflammation of the sclera, frequently immune-mediated and often a manifestation of systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease. Immune-complex deposition and T-cell-mediated inflammation cause oedema and cellular infiltration of the sclera and episclera; in necrotising disease, occlusive vasculitis of the deep episcleral vessels leads to scleral ischaemia, necrosis, and thinning, with risk of perforation. Chronic or severe inflammation can extend to adjacent structures causing keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma, and, in posterior disease, exudative retinal detachment and optic nerve involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital cellulitis or orbital inflammatory disease (posterior scleritis)
Choroidal tumour or exudative retinal detachment (posterior scleritis)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination with assessment of deep vessel involvement and response to topical phenylephrine
B-scan ultrasonography for posterior scleritis (scleral thickening and T-sign)
Inflammatory and autoimmune workup: full blood count, ESR/CRP, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor
Investigations for infective causes (including syphilis and tuberculosis) when indicated
Imaging or systemic referral when an underlying vasculitis is suspected
redFlags: Necrotising scleritis with scleral thinning or threatened perforation
Severe pain with reduced vision indicating posterior segment or optic nerve involvement
Features of systemic vasculitis (e.g. granulomatosis with polyangiitis) requiring urgent systemic treatment
Rapid progression despite therapy suggesting infective scleritis or aggressive vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Diffuse and nodular anterior scleritis usually respond to anti-inflammatory treatment with good visual outcomes, but necrotising scleritis is associated with significant ocular morbidity and, when linked to systemic vasculitis, increased mortality if the underlying disease is untreated.
pitfalls: Mistaking scleritis for the benign, self-limiting episcleritis and undertreating it
Failing to search for and treat an underlying systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease
Missing posterior scleritis, which lacks obvious external redness and mimics orbital disease
Using topical steroids alone when systemic immunosuppression is required for necrotising disease
